newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia quiet, royalists fearful after execution.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia quiet, royalists fearful after execution.

text.p: Several leading Cambodian royalist officials were in hiding on Wednesday after the execution of a colleague arrested by troops loyal to strongman Hun Sen who now control the capital Phnom Penh.

Although Cambodia was quiet following weekend fighting in Phnom Penh that later spread to the countryside, a second day of evacuation flights organised by Southeast Asian neighbours carried hundreds more to safety from this tense capital.

The United States condemned Second Prime Minister Hun Sen for using force to oust First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, his partner in an uneasy four-year-old coalition and son of King Norodom Sihanouk. It said U.S. officials in Washington would meet Ranariddh, now in Paris.

Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas said the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN), whose foreign ministers meet on Thursday on the situation, had not ruled out postponing Cambodian membership slated for later this month.

Phnom Penh was calm overnight, apart from isolated and apparently random gunfire, and there were no reports of major new clashes in the provinces, officials and witnesses said. Acording to preliminary reports, 58 people died and almost 200 were wounded -- mostly civilians -- in the weekend fighting in Phnom Penh.

A number of top officials from Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party were hiding after strongman Hun Sen's forces arrested and executed senior Ranariddh loyalist Ho Sok, party officials said on Wednesday.
Hun Sen's troops arrested Ho Sok, who was interior ministry secretary of state, on Monday and he was later shot dead, an interior ministry official told reporters.

Khieu Sopheak, an interior ministry adviser loyal to Hun Sen, said Ho Sok had been involved in "sabotage and plots" and "was shot down by the people that were angry with him". He did not say when Ho Sok was killed or exactly who had killed him.
The execution sparked fear amongst Ranariddh loyalists in the capital.
Ho Sok was among four senior FUNCINPEC members identified by Hun Sen as being responsible for the weekend fighting. Hun Sen said the four had to be hunted down and arrested.
The other three FUNCINPEC loyalists named by Hun Sen were Ranariddh's top military man top Nhiek Bun Chaay, FUNCINPEC security official Serey Kosal and Chao Sambath, a party intelligence official.
There were unconfirmed reports on Wednesday that Chao Sambath had been arrested.

Several human rights organisations, including Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, condemned the execution and urged the global community to take all necessary measures to prevent any purge of FUNCINPEC officials.

A local government official in the northwestern city of Battambang said there had been no fresh fighting in that area between forces loyal to the rival premiers. Some fighting had been reported on Tuesday.

Aid workers reported a clash between police and soldiers in the central Cambodian town of Pursat on Wednesday morning. The reason for the clash was not immediately clear and there was no immediate official confirmation.

The northern tourist town of Siem Reap was also quiet, sources in the town said, a day after fighting in the area prompted evacuation to Phnom Penh by helicopter of some 200 people, including many foreign tourists.
The town, close to the fabled 12th century Angkor Wat ruins, is Cambodia's main tourist attraction.

Thailand evacuated almost 800 people, the majority of them Thai, from Phnom Penh on Tuesday in the first mercy flights. Two aircraft from Singapore flew in to pick up evacuees on Wednesday morning, an embassy official said. Other military aircraft were due in from the Philippines and Malaysia.
Phnom Penh airport, which has been closed since Saturday to commercial flights, was set to reopen later on Wednesday.

Keo Sophal, secretary general of the Civil Aviation Department, said commercial flights were to resume on a limited basis. "Domestic flights will start today. There are four domestic flights, to Siem Reap and Battambang, and two flights to Ho Chi Minh City."
Airlines could not confirm any flights for Wednesday.
Cambodia was plunged into turmoil on Saturday when forces under powerful Second Prime Minister Hun Sen moved against Ranariddh's men in the capital.
After two days of heavy fighting in the city centre and its outskirts, Hun Sen declared that Ranariddh, who left Phnom Penh on the eve of the fighting, had been ousted from his job.

Hun Sen, leader of the former communist, Hanoi-backed government which ruled the country until a 1991 peace treaty and United Nations peace process, was a former member of the Khmer Rouge who broke with the Maoist group during their "killing fields" rule in the late 1970s and fled to Vietnam.
The weekend fighting began after Hun Sen accused Ranariddh of smuggling defectors from the Khmer Rouge guerrilla group into the capital. The prince denied the accusation.
Breakaway Khmer Rouge sources said on Wednesday that Hun Sen had sent large numbers of extra troops to western Cambodia to prevent Ranariddh forces linking up with hardline Khmer Rouge guerrillas.

The sources, who were monitoring troop movements inside Cambodia by field radio, said the forces of Second Prime Minister Hun Sen had succeeded in blocking various routes between the town of Poipet on Cambodia's border with Thailand and the northwestern province of Siem Reap.
